Iceberg

Geophysics OurBigBook.com
An iceberg is a detached mass of freshwater ice floating in the ocean.

Iceberg melt heat budget (Q=∫ρi​[Lf​+ci​(Tm​−Ti​)]dV)

Words: 90 Articles: 1
Iceberg OurBigBook.com
For an initially cold iceberg, melting to liquid at temperature Tm​ requires both latent heat of fusion Lf​ and sensible warming determined by the ice specific heat capacity ci​. Spatial mass density and temperature profiles determine their mass-weighted integrals. Additional warming of the meltwater requires a separate heat contribution.

Poleward heat transport by equatorward iceberg drift (Q˙​=N˙Q)

Words: 49
Iceberg melt heat budget OurBigBook.com
An iceberg moving toward the equator carries a thermal deficit into warmer water. Melting extracts heat there, equivalent to transport of heat toward the pole. For an annual number of similar bergs, multiply their individual iceberg melt heat budget by the rate per second. Freshwater effects on density stratification and ocean circulation are separate from this heat accounting.

Iceberg freeboard (F=H−ρw−1​∫0H​ρi​(z)dz)

Words: 41
Iceberg OurBigBook.com
For a vertical-sided floating iceberg of height H, Archimedes' principle equates displaced water mass to ice mass. Its draft is ρw−1​∫0H​ρi​(z)dz and its freeboard is the remaining height above water. A depth-dependent mass density must be integrated; using the densest layer throughout overestimates the draft.

Iceberg free drift

Words: 133 Articles: 2
Iceberg OurBigBook.com
The free-drift velocity of an iceberg follows from air and water drag, the Coriolis force, pressure gradients, currents and other external forces. Large submerged area and mass make its wind response weak compared with that of a thin floe.

Damped free drift of an iceberg (v˙+fJv+γv=F/m)

Words: 62
Iceberg free drift OurBigBook.com
For a constant wind force F, still water, and linear water drag force −mγv, let Jv=z^×v. The Coriolis parameter f gives equilibrium v∞​=(γF−fJF)/[m(γ2+f2)]. The deviation evolves as e−γtR(−ft)(v(0)−v∞​), a damped inertial oscillation. Actual drag is commonly quadratic, so this is a linear illustrative model rather than a universal iceberg speed law.

Iceberg towing drag (FD​=21​ρCD​AU2)

Words: 33
Iceberg free drift OurBigBook.com
Water drag on a large iceberg can exceed a tug force by many orders of magnitude; the relevant area is the immersed horizontal base when the quoted coefficient is an equivalent water-drag coefficient.

Open-ocean convection

Words: 70 Articles: 1
Geophysics OurBigBook.com

Convective chimney

Words: 70
Open-ocean convection OurBigBook.com
A convective chimney is a localized deeply mixed region formed when surface buoyancy loss overcomes ocean density stratification. Small plumes, compensating flow, rotation and lateral exchange maintain its structure; it need not be a permanently uniform descending column. Brine rejection can increase its surface density forcing. A fresh summer cap can isolate a deep homogeneous core until winter forcing renews contact with the surface, so a surviving core need not imply continuous active convection.

Loss of bright sea ice exposes dark ocean, increasing absorbed solar radiation, delaying autumn refreezing and causing further ice loss.

Sea ice thermodynamics

Words: 836 Articles: 16
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
The thermodynamics of sea ice couples conductive heat transport, radiative and turbulent surface fluxes, basal ocean heat and latent heat of freezing and melting.

Basal melt heat flux (Fmelt​=ρi​Lf​Δh/Δt)

Words: 43
Sea ice thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
Melting a basal ice thickness Δh consumes energy ρi​Lf​Δh per unit area, ignoring sensible warming and salinity corrections. The corresponding time-averaged heat flux is this energy divided by Δt. The actual ocean heat flux also includes heat conducted into the ice.
// Target: geophysics.bigb

Freezing degree-day (N=∫max(Tf​−Ta​,0)dt)

Words: 102 Articles: 1
Sea ice thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
A freezing degree-day accumulates air temperature below a declared reference freezing temperature, with time in days and temperature difference in degrees Celsius or kelvins. The reference temperature and averaging convention must match the empirical sea ice thermodynamics formula using it. Warming by a constant ΔT subtracts ΔT times the number of days only if those days remain below the reference threshold.

Lebedev ice-growth law (H=0.0133N0.58)

Words: 42
Freezing degree-day OurBigBook.com
This empirical sea ice growth relation gives thickness H in metres from accumulated freezing degree-days N. Its coefficient includes the specified units and calibration. It is not a complete energy-balance model: snow, ocean heat and changing forcing can alter its applicability. Inversion gives N=(H/0.0133)1/0.58.

Water-equivalent thickness (hw​=ρi​hi​/ρw,ref​)

Words: 85
Sea ice thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
The water-equivalent thickness expresses an ice mass per area as a depth of water at a declared reference density. With mi​=ρi​hi​ per area, hw​=mi​/ρw,ref​. Ice at 900 kgm−3 and thickness 2.44 m has about 2.20 m water equivalent at a fresh-water reference density of 1000 kgm−3. The depth of seawater consumed at 1025 kgm−3 is instead about 2.14 m. A reference depth must not replace ice thickness in an ice-volume calculation or the liquid mass removed in brine rejection.

Brine rejection

Words: 386 Articles: 8
Sea ice thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
When seawater freezes, most salt remains in liquid, increasing salinity and density and potentially driving convection.

Migration of brine inclusions

Words: 39
Brine rejection OurBigBook.com
A temperature gradient can move a brine inclusion by melting its warmer wall and freezing its colder wall. This slow process can redistribute salt, but is generally much less effective at net desalination than gravity drainage of sea-ice brine or meltwater flushing of sea ice.
// Target: geophysics.bigb

Brine expulsion

Words: 35
Brine rejection OurBigBook.com
Freezing within a brine inclusion expands the solid fraction and can force concentrated liquid into neighboring pores or channels. Expulsion redistributes salt internally; net desalination requires a path crossing the ice boundary.
// Target: geophysics.bigb

Meltwater flushing of sea ice

Words: 34
Brine rejection OurBigBook.com
Surface meltwater with a positive hydraulic head can percolate through permeable sea ice, displacing brine into the ocean. Flushing can efficiently desalinate warm summer ice, but requires meltwater and connected flow paths.
// Target: geophysics.bigb

Gravity drainage of sea-ice brine

Words: 34
Brine rejection OurBigBook.com
Dense saline liquid in connected pore space can drain from sea ice while fresher seawater enters. The process is controlled by buoyancy, permeability of a porous medium and network connectivity, and is a major means of growing-ice desalination.
// Target: geophysics.bigb

Conservation of salt during freezing (S1​=S0​/(1−fi​))

Words: 190 Articles: 2
Brine rejection OurBigBook.com
If a fraction fi​ of initial liquid mass freezes into salt-free ice, all original salt remains in a liquid mass fraction 1−fi​. Writing salinity as salt concentration per mass gives S1​(1−fi​)=S0​, hence ΔS=S0​fi​/(1−fi​). For equal initial cooling and subsequent freezing heat extraction, fi​=cp,w​ΔT/Lf​. The liquid specific heat capacity, rather than the ice value, determines the initial heat removal. If ice retains salt, the mass balance instead reads S1​(1−fi​)+Si​fi​=S0​.
Conservation of salt with salt-retaining ice (S/S0​=(M/M0​)r−1)
Words: 62
Conservation of salt during freezing OurBigBook.com
Let liquid mass M freeze incrementally, and let each new ice increment retain salinity rS with constant 0≤r≤1, where S is the instantaneous well-mixed liquid salinity. Conservation gives d(MS)=rSdM, hence dS/S=(r−1)dM/M. Integrating yields S/S0​=(M/M0​)r−1. For frozen mass fraction f, ΔS=S0​[(1−f)−(1−r)−1]≃(1−r)S0​f. Specifying a fixed bulk ice salinity instead produces a different, though first-order compatible, finite-mass balance.
Freezing-to-cooling density efficiency (R=(∂ρ/∂S)S0​fi​/((1−fi​)∣∂ρ/∂T∣ΔT))
Words: 54
Conservation of salt during freezing OurBigBook.com
For equal heat extraction, the density increase caused by brine rejection can exceed that caused by cooling near the freezing point because the thermal density response is weak. Using conservation of salt during freezing, the ratio is R=(∂ρ/∂S)S0​fi​/[(1−fi​)∣∂ρ/∂T∣ΔT], with fi​=cp,w​ΔT/Lf​. This is a parcel comparison, not a guarantee that freezing overcomes any ambient density stratification.

Freezing density increase (Δρ≃ΔS)

Words: 38
Brine rejection OurBigBook.com
For the conversion used in the exam, rejected salt increases density about one kilogram per cubic metre per practical salinity unit. The same heat loss can therefore produce much denser water through freezing than through modest sensible cooling.

Maykut-Untersteiner model

Words: 198 Articles: 2
Sea ice thermodynamics OurBigBook.com
The Maykut-Untersteiner model is a seasonally forced one-dimensional sea ice thermodynamics model with snow and saline ice layers. It couples radiative and turbulent surface fluxes, heat conduction, interior shortwave absorption, brine-dependent effective heat capacity and conductivity, snowfall, and a basal Stefan condition driven by prescribed ocean heat flux. Its annual sea-ice thermodynamic equilibrium is a periodic cycle with zero net yearly thickness change. The snow insulation and summer ice protection mechanisms compete, so additional snow need not reduce annual equilibrium thickness. The transient temperature profile need not be linear.

Snow insulation and summer ice protection

Words: 61
Maykut-Untersteiner model OurBigBook.com
At fixed boundary temperatures, a snow cover decreases winter conductive heat loss through the resistance hs​/ks​+hi​/ki​ and inhibits sea ice growth. Its high albedo and persistence into summer reduce ablation. Therefore annual equilibrium thickness has competing snow sensitivities. The near cancellation at modest snow depth and thickening with persistent summer snow in the original Maykut-Untersteiner model are forcing-dependent responses, not a universal monotonically decreasing snow-thickness relation.

Annual sea-ice thermodynamic equilibrium (h(t+T)=h(t))

Words: 66
Maykut-Untersteiner model OurBigBook.com
For annually repeated forcing, a thermodynamic equilibrium is a periodic temperature field and thickness cycle. The yearly integral of net ice growth is zero, although substantial winter growth and summer ablation can each occur. Equilibrium thickness must specify an annual mean or a phase of the cycle. A change in forcing can remove a perennial-ice solution without making every transient thickness decrease at the same rate.

Oil spill under sea ice

Words: 120 Articles: 1
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
An oil spill beneath sea ice is transported by a rising buoyant plume, lateral currents and the evolving ice--water interface. A slick can be spread, trapped in ridges, incorporated into growing ice or released through brine channels and melt ponds.

Ice-floe oil painting fraction (min{1,Q/(dvh)})

Words: 83
Oil spill under sea ice OurBigBook.com
If a buoyant plume of diameter d supplies oil at volume rate Q to an ice floe moving at speed v, the plume sweeps area dv per unit time. Retaining a layer of depth h over that area would require volume rate dvh, so conservation of mass gives the painted fraction min{1,Q/(dvh)}. Discontinuous painting starts when v>Q/(dh). This estimate assumes all arriving oil is retained and a constant track width equal to the plume diameter; the plume's circular cross-sectional area does not enter the swept-area rate.

Permafrost

Words: 101 Articles: 2
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Permafrost is ground that remains at or below its freezing threshold for at least two consecutive years. Thaw can expose previously frozen organic material to decomposition, with methanogenesis where conditions are anaerobic.

Permafrost carbon feedback

Words: 49
Permafrost OurBigBook.com
Thawing permafrost makes previously frozen organic matter available for decomposition, releasing carbon dioxide and, in waterlogged oxygen-poor conditions, methane. These greenhouse gases amplify warming, which can cause further thaw. The amount reaching the atmosphere depends on decomposition, transport and oxidation; this feedback does not imply an inevitable abrupt release of an entire carbon reservoir.

Thermokarst

Words: 21
Permafrost OurBigBook.com
Thermokarst is subsidence and related landscape change caused by thaw of ice-rich permafrost. Resulting lakes and saturated sediments can promote methanogenesis.

Climate change

Words: 743 Articles: 15
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Climate change is a persistent alteration of the statistical behaviour of a planet's climate. External forcing and climate feedbacks both matter, and the timescale must be specified.

Polar amplification

Words: 47
Climate change OurBigBook.com
Polar amplification is greater temperature change at high latitudes than in the global mean. Ice-albedo feedback, the vertical structure of atmospheric warming, the temperature dependence of radiative cooling, ocean heat storage, clouds and energy transport all contribute; the balance differs between the Arctic and Antarctic and between seasons.

Attribution of recent climate change

Words: 53
Climate change OurBigBook.com
Attribution of recent climate change assesses the contributions of anthropogenic forcing, natural forcing and internal variability to observed changes. It combines the physics of radiative transfer, measured forcing agents, energy budgets and spatial, vertical and temporal response patterns. A single weather event or a single trend is insufficient by itself to identify all causes.

Global warming

Words: 39
Climate change OurBigBook.com
Global warming is an increase in Earth's global mean surface temperature. It is one aspect of climate change, which also includes changes in precipitation, circulation, extremes and the cryosphere. Warming driven by additional greenhouse gases can be amplified or moderated by climate feedbacks.

Sea level rise (η˙​)

Words: 238 Articles: 4
Climate change OurBigBook.com
Global mean sea level can rise through changes in ocean volume at fixed mass and through additions of ocean mass. Local relative sea level additionally depends on ocean circulation, gravity and vertical motion of the land. Floating sea ice has already displaced seawater, so its melt has a much smaller direct sea-level effect than transfer of grounded land ice into the ocean.

Words: 63

Gravity-driven ice flow on a conical slope OurBigBook.com
For an initially bare cone with accumulation a≃A near its apex, the early outer thickness is At. The radial gravity flux becomes comparable to accumulation over distance xa​∼DA2t3. Setting h=AtF(η) and η=x/(DA2t3) gives
F−3ηF′=1−η1​(ηF3)′,F(∞)=1.
(33)
Regular apex flux requires F∼(η/2)1/3 near zero. The boundary layer therefore approaches the local steady thickness (Ax/(2D))1/3 while farther regions are still filling.

Ice divide

Words: 28
Ice sheet dynamics OurBigBook.com
An ice divide is a line or point of maximum ice-surface elevation from which ice flows in opposite directions. Symmetry gives zero horizontal ice flux at the divide.

Snowline

Words: 31
Ice sheet dynamics OurBigBook.com
The snowline separates a region of net annual snow accumulation from a region of net ablation. A height-based idealization places it where the ice surface has a prescribed elevation h∗.

Basal sliding

Words: 163 Articles: 3
Ice sheet dynamics OurBigBook.com
Basal sliding is motion of glacier ice relative to its bed. A sliding law relates the basal velocity to basal shear stress, effective pressure, roughness, or other bed properties.
Linear basal drag law (σb​=μβub​)
Words: 44
Basal sliding OurBigBook.com
A linear basal drag law has resisting traction −μβub​, with β>0 of dimension inverse length. It idealizes lubrication by subglacial till and is equivalent to a Navier slip boundary condition of slip length 1/β when the ice is a Newtonian fluid. It is a constitutive idealization, not a universal sliding law.
Subglacial till
Words: 90 Articles: 1
Basal sliding OurBigBook.com
Subglacial till is a mixture of rock fragments and fine sediment beneath ice. A wet deformable layer can lubricate basal sliding. Its constitutive equation must be specified; Newtonian till lubrication is one idealization, rather than a claim that all subglacial till is a Newtonian fluid.
Newtonian till lubrication (τb​=λμu/l)
Words: 52
Subglacial till OurBigBook.com
A thin layer of subglacial till idealized as a Newtonian fluid of dynamic viscosity λμ and thickness l undergoes Couette flow between stationary bedrock and ice moving at speed u. Its resisting basal shear stress has magnitude τb​=λμu/l and acts opposite to the sliding motion. Combining this drag with the hydrostatic driving force gives the bulk approximation used in the friction-dominated grounding-line evolution law.

Ice shelf

Words: 616 Articles: 11
Ice sheet dynamics OurBigBook.com
An ice shelf is the floating extension of a grounded ice sheet. Hydrostatic flotation makes its surface slope and horizontal driving stress depend on the density contrast between ice and seawater.
Ice-shelf buttressing
Words: 51
Ice shelf OurBigBook.com
Ice-shelf buttressing is the restraint that a floating ice shelf, through its contact with sidewalls or pinning points, can exert on upstream grounded ice flow. Thinning or loss of the shelf can reduce this restraint and increase discharge, but the response depends on geometry and cannot be inferred from floating-ice area alone.
Ice-shelf water
Words: 53
Ice shelf OurBigBook.com
Ice-shelf water has acquired characteristic properties through interaction with the underside of an ice shelf. Melting at depth can cool and freshen the water, including cooling below the surface freezing temperature because pressure lowers the freezing point. Its eventual density and contribution to deep-water formation depend on mixing with surrounding shelf and ocean waters.
Grounding line
Words: 401 Articles: 6
Ice shelf OurBigBook.com
The grounding line is the transition where an ice sheet detaches from its bed and begins to float as an ice shelf. Ice thickness there obeys the hydrostatic flotation condition.
Ice-sheet flotation (ρH=ρw​b)
Words: 56
Grounding line OurBigBook.com
At a grounding line, hydrostatic pressures balance when the weight of an ice column of thickness H and mass density ρ equals the weight of its displaced water, of depth b and mass density ρw​. Thus flotation gives ρH=ρw​b. Its time derivative along a moving grounding line relates local thickness changes to grounding-line speed; it supplies a different boundary condition from the unbuttressed Newtonian grounding-line stress.
Friction-dominated grounding-line evolution law ([αρw​/ρ−Hx​]x˙G​)
Words: 192 Articles: 1
Grounding line OurBigBook.com
For a bed depth b=αx, a thin subglacial till layer of thickness l is idealized by Newtonian till lubrication, with dynamic viscosity λμ and basal drag λμu/l. Neglecting longitudinal stress divergence in the bulk yields u=−(l/λ)(g/ν)Hhx​. Retaining the unbuttressed Newtonian grounding-line stress condition as boundary data and differentiating ice-sheet flotation along the moving grounding line gives
(αρρw​​−Hx​)x˙G​=λl​νg​Hhx​(hx​+α)−8νg′H2​.
(34)
Indeed, mass conservation gives Ht​=−uHx​−Hux​, Hx​=hx​+α, and ice-sheet flotation gives Ht​=(αρw​/ρ−Hx​)x˙G​. This is a formal local friction closure, not a uniformly valid removal of membrane stress near every grounding line. If the coefficient of x˙G​ vanishes, it is an implicit compatibility condition and cannot be divided to obtain a finite speed.
Steady friction-dominated grounding-line thickness relation (8gg′​H5=Q(Q−αH2))
Words: 88
Friction-dominated grounding-line evolution law OurBigBook.com
With constant volume flux per unit width Hu=q0​>0, define β=l/λ, H=H/β, and Q=νq0​/(gβ3). The friction closure gives Hx​=α−q0​ν/(βgH2). Differentiating constant flux and applying the unbuttressed Newtonian grounding-line stress condition gives q0​Hx​/H+g′H2/(8ν)=0. Substitution proves the displayed relation. For α≥0, g′>0 and Q>0, the polynomial (g′/8g)H5+αQH2−Q2 increases strictly on the positive half-line, begins negative and tends to infinity; hence it has exactly one positive root. Its root satisfies Q>αH2, so the thickness decreases seaward at that steady grounding line.
Unbuttressed Newtonian grounding-line stress (4μHux​=ρg′H2/2)
Words: 59
Grounding line OurBigBook.com
For a two-dimensional Newtonian fluid ice sheet attached to an unbuttressed ice shelf, ice-sheet flotation gives ρH=ρw​b. The difference between the depth-integrated ice and ocean hydrostatic pressures is ρgH2/2−ρw​gb2/2=ρg′H2/2, where g′=g(1−ρ/ρw​). Shelf force balance integrates 4μHux​−ρg′H2/2 to a constant; absence of a buttressing force makes that constant zero. The shallow-shelf approximation therefore gives the displayed boundary condition, or ux​=g′H/(8ν) with kinematic viscosity ν=μ/ρ.
Newtonian grounding-line flux
Words: 31
Grounding line OurBigBook.com
Matching a slowly varying grounded Newtonian sheet to a freely extending Newtonian shelf gives, in a standard two-dimensional model,
qG​=6νgg′​​hG3​,
(35)
where hG​ is the flotation thickness and g′=g(ρw​−ρ)/ρw​ is the reduced gravity.
Shelfy stream
Words: 34
Grounding line OurBigBook.com
A shelfy stream is a grounded, rapidly sliding ice stream whose internal resistance is dominated by longitudinal extension, as in an ice shelf, but which retains a basal drag. It is described by the shallow-shelf approximation.
Shallow-shelf approximation
Words: 37
Ice shelf OurBigBook.com
The shallow-shelf approximation treats horizontal velocity as nearly depth-independent and balances membrane stress, hydrostatic driving stress, and basal traction. For Newtonian ice of thickness h and speed u, the extensional resultant is 4μhux​.
Ice-shelf corrugation relaxation
Words: 43
Ice shelf OurBigBook.com
Short-wavelength corrugations on the underside of a highly viscous ice shelf relax through local Stokes flow. For a wavelength much smaller than the shelf thickness, the deformation occupies a depth of order the inverse wavenumber and the ice may be treated as a viscous half-space.

Postglacial rebound

Words: 124 Articles: 4
Geophysics OurBigBook.com
Postglacial rebound is uplift following removal of an ice load. It reflects viscous flow in the mantle and elastic or viscoelastic deformation of the lithosphere.

Glacial isostatic adjustment

Words: 99 Articles: 3
Postglacial rebound OurBigBook.com
Glacial isostatic adjustment is the broader solid-Earth and sea-level response to growth and retreat of ice sheets.

Flexural isostasy

Words: 37
Glacial isostatic adjustment OurBigBook.com
Flexural isostasy models the lithosphere as an elastic plate that bends over a buoyant substrate. For a sinusoidal deflection of wavenumber k, bending contributes a restoring stress proportional to Bk4, where B is the plate's bending stiffness.

Laurentide Ice Sheet

Words: 23
Glacial isostatic adjustment OurBigBook.com
The Laurentide Ice Sheet covered much of northern North America during the last glacial period and left a major postglacial-rebound signal after retreat.

Fennoscandian Ice Sheet

Words: 22
Glacial isostatic adjustment OurBigBook.com
The Fennoscandian Ice Sheet covered northern Europe during the last glacial period and produced ongoing uplift around the Baltic region after retreat.
